schools.summary: Keil frames the verse as the title of the first list, its twenty-two heads recurring (with clerical variations) as the priestly houses of vv.12-21; Ellicott takes Seraiah as the family name represented by Jeshua and owns nothing more is known of Jeremiah and Ezra.
Henry reads the long roll as a memorial of faithful ministers, that posterity might know their debt (Ps. 112:6; Heb. 13:7).

Wesley and Clarke fix these as the chief of the twenty-four Davidic courses (1 Chron. 24), thinned to twenty-two by the captivity; Clarke calls the list the chief, not the whole, and notes the LXX omissions.
Gill fixes Zerubbabel the prince and Jeshua the high priest at the head of the returning company.

debates.question: Is the 'Ezra' named here Ezra the scribe?

sides.position: the same Ezra the scribe, preserved by providence to a great age
not the famous scribe, or now beyond recovery

schools.summary: Gill finds these names among the sealers of the covenant (Neh. 10) and marks the Malluch here as the Melicu of v.14.
Keil sets the twenty-two heads as the houses that recur in vv.12-21; Ellicott reads them as family names, not individuals, so a name may pass down generations.

Wesley grounds the count in David's twenty-four courses (1 Chron. 24), thinned to twenty-two by the captivity and to twenty in v.12 where Hattush left no posterity; Clarke calls the list the chief, not the whole.
Henry keeps the memorial purpose of the register before the reader.
Ellicott reads the 'and' before Joiarib as beginning the list of those who did not seal the covenant (cf. v.19); Keil notes fifteen of the twenty-two heads had sealed it (Neh. 10).
Gill sets the names among the sealers and the chief priests whose courses the return was restoring.
Wesley keeps the frame of the twenty-four courses (1 Chron. 24) thinned by the captivity, each name standing for a ministering house.
Henry presses the memorial worth of the record, a debt owed to faithful guides (Heb. 13:7).

themes: sealers and non-sealers of the covenant

schools.summary: Clarke fixes the four-and-twenty courses David established (1 Chron. 24), continuing to the Roman destruction of Jerusalem; Wesley counts the twenty-two the return could muster.

Ellicott grants 'chief' genealogically but not by the courses, which are complete in none of the lists; Keil reads the verse as the subscription sealing the first list, the brethren being the Levites.
Gill keeps the arithmetic of the courses, twenty-two of David's twenty-four surviving the exile.

debates.question: Does this list of chief priests preserve David's twenty-four courses?

sides.position: the courses David established, continuing in force to Roman times
genealogical heads only; the courses are complete in none of the lists

themes: the subscription of the first list

schools.summary: Clarke glosses 'over the thanksgiving' as chief of the principal singers (Neh. 11:17); Wesley reads it as a standing trust to keep the psalms of thanksgiving continually sung in due order.
Keil sets the Levitical heads among the sealers of Neh. 10, takes 'Judah' as miswritten for Hodiah, and identifies Mattaniah the Asaphite (Neh. 11:17) as over the singing of praise.
Gill fixes these as the Levites who lived in the same generation as the priests just listed.

themes: the continual song of the temple

schools.summary: Keil reads 'over against them in the watches' as the answering choir, not watch-posts (forbidden by v.24), and notes Unni is met with nowhere else yet is not to be emended away.
Gill marks two further Levites, the first named again in the muster of Neh. 11:17.
Keil sets the genealogy as a connecting link fixing the dates of the several lists, and takes 'Jonathan' for a clerical error for Johanan, who (per Josephus) murdered his brother in the temple.
Wesley reads the succession of high priests as a necessary calendar, the times of the second temple now measured by high priests and not by kings.
Gill judges the paragraph a later inspired insertion, since Nehemiah could scarcely have lived to Jaddua's meeting with Alexander.

outliers.note: Holds the high-priestly genealogy, reaching to Jaddua and Alexander's day, to be a later inspired insertion by another hand, as with similar insertions in Moses and Joshua, since Nehemiah could hardly have lived so long.

schools.summary: Ellicott corrects Jonathan to Johanan (v.22) and takes Jaddua for the high priest who met Alexander; Keil reads the succession as fixing the dates of the Levitical lists.
Clarke recovers the scene of Jaddua meeting Alexander in pontifical robes after Tyre and Gaza, so that the conqueror spared Jerusalem (Josephus, Prideaux).
Gill draws from the reach to Alexander's day his conclusion that the passage is a later inspired hand.
Gill identifies Joiakim as Jeshua's son and counts twenty heads against the fathers' twenty-two, Hattush and Miamin leaving no descendants.
Wesley reads the sons executing the priesthood in their fathers' room, some fathers living and many dead.
Keil sets the houses of vv.12-21 as answering, with slight variations, to the heads of vv.1-7.
Henry blesses the providence by which one generation of ministers succeeds another — the rare mercy of twenty good sons filling twenty good fathers' places.
Keil lays the roll beside vv.1-7 house by house; Ellicott notes the names do not always answer cleanly (Melicu for Malluch, a dropped name), anomalies of which no account can now be given.
Gill keeps the tally of twenty heads against twenty-two, Hattush and Miamin failing of descendants.
Henry redeems the dry column with the wonder that twenty good fathers should leave twenty good sons to fill their places.

themes: God who never leaves his house without a servant

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies Melicu as the Malluch of v.2 and notes Hattush omitted, anomalies of which no account can be given; Keil files the divergences under clerical error.
Gill accounts for the vanished Hattush, whose house left no posterity, so that twenty heads stand where the fathers had twenty-two.
Wesley likewise traces the missing Hattush to a house extinct without descendants.
Ellicott notes that against Miniamin 'some name has dropped out'; Keil sets the loss among the clerical slips of a hand-copied text.
Gill keeps the register's character, the houses named by ancestor, most otherwise unknown.
Henry lifts the damaged line to its memorial purpose — to know what our godly predecessors were.

themes: the imperfection of the transmitted list

schools.summary: Keil reads the verse as both the title of the Levite list and the subscription of the priest list, recorded 'under the reign of Darius the Persian.'
Gill fixes Eliashib as the third high priest of the second temple, in whose days the list was drawn.
Clarke rehearses Jaddua meeting Alexander and sets out the rival Dariuses; Wesley chooses Darius Nothus, making this Jaddua the father of the one in Alexander's day.

debates.question: Which Darius the Persian is meant?

sides.position: Darius Codomanus, the last king, defeated by Alexander

schools.summary: Keil sets the chief Levites to praise and give thanks according to David (1 Chron. 16:4; 23:30), 'ward over against ward,' and would expunge the 'ben' before Kadmiel as a gloss.
Clarke insists 'the book of the chronicles' is not the canonical Chronicles, no such list being found there, but a lost register.
Gill reports that some refer the phrase to the canonical Chronicles.

debates.question: What is 'the book of the chronicles' cited here?

sides.position: a lost official register, not the canonical Chronicles
the canonical Chronicles, as some hold

schools.summary: Ellicott hears the account resume with the Levites, the names largely recurring; Keil sets the answering companies to praise and give thanks per David (1 Chron. 23:30), ward over against ward.
Gill marks the point where Nehemiah's history is carried on from the priests to the Levites.
Keil marks v.26 as the final subscription of the two lists; Ellicott glosses 'at the thresholds' as at the treasuries, the store-chambers attached to the gates.
Clarke, puzzled by the notion of porticoes, proposes rather watch-boxes or moveable shelters for the gate-keepers.
Gill sets the porters keeping watch at the gates of the temple.

debates.question: What were the 'thresholds' the porters kept?

sides.position: watch-boxes or moveable shelters at the gates
the treasuries or store-chambers attached to the gates

schools.summary: Gill traces the descent from Jozadak, high priest in Babylon, to his grandson Joiakim in the restored temple.
Keil fixes the verse as the final subscription dating both lists to Joiakim, Nehemiah, and Ezra.
Henry sees in the whole register a memorial of God's care, its singers and porters set according to the command of David.
Henry reads the dedication as thanksgiving, a devoting of the holy city to God (Ps. 48:2; Matt. 5:35), and a putting of it under his protection (Ps. 127:1) — sowing in tears, reaping in joy.
Keil marks the wall finished (Neh. 6:15) and now dedicated with gladness (cf. Ezra 6:16); Ellicott makes the solemnity processional, musical, and sacrificial after Solomon's pattern.
Wesley reads the holy city given back to God who chose and sanctified it; Clarke notes the ancients too consecrated their cities and walls to their gods.
Gill takes the dedication for a festival of prayer, praise, and sacrifice, kept yearly on the seventh of Elul.

outliers.note: Adduces Ovid's account of Romulus founding Rome — the heathen consecration of city walls to the gods — as a pagan shadow of Israel's true dedication.

themes: the holy city devoted to God
except the Lord keep the city

schools.summary: Keil identifies the three Levitical companies of singers (Neh. 11:17) gathered from the Jordan valley and the villages of Netophathi (1 Chron. 9:16).
Gill takes 'the sons of the singers' for the singing Levites and their sons trained to the office.
Henry notes the Levites summoned from all parts of the country to the dedication.
Keil traces the companies to Beth-gilgal and the fields of Geba and Azmaveth; Ellicott sets the Levitical singers chiefly in villages north of the city.
Clarke reads Beth-Gilgal as the village where Israel encamped after crossing Jordan under Joshua.
Gill places Gilgal in the plains of Jericho.

Ellicott insists on purification before consecration, by offerings and ablutions (2 Chron. 29:15; Ezra 6:20), the gates and wall sprinkled; Keil judges it done by sin- and burnt-offerings (2 Chron. 29:20).
Clarke describes washings and abstinence, and the removing of filth and rubbish; Wesley: those who would sanctify others must first sanctify themselves.
Gill takes the purifying to be by washing of body and clothes and sprinkling the water of purification.
Henry: cleanse hands and hearts when any work for God passes through them; the sprinkled water a type of the blood of Christ (Heb. 9:14; Num. 19:9).

themes: purification of self, people, gates, wall

schools.summary: Keil sets two great companies of thanks going in opposite directions to meet at the house of God; Ellicott fixes the muster on the south-west wall before the division.
Clarke lays out the order of the march from the dung gate, right and left, to the great space by the temple; Wesley sends half the people with the princes toward the south and east.
Gill notes the wall broad enough to walk upon, the princes of Benjamin included.
Henry sees the two companies with music, Ezra and Nehemiah leading, meeting at last in the temple.
Keil lists the file of princes and the priests' sons with trumpets; Ellicott marks the mingling of the clerical and lay elements in the procession.
Gill sets Hoshaiah at the head of the other half of the princes of Judah.
Henry fixes Ezra leading the van of the first company.

themes: the composition of the first company

schools.summary: Gill warns this Ezra is not the priest and scribe (who has his place at v.36) but one of the princes.
Ellicott suggests this Ezra is probably the same as the preceding Azariah; Keil files the names among the princes of the first company.
Henry keeps the first company moving toward the house of God.
Gill, with Jarchi, takes Judah and Benjamin for the personal names of two princes, not the tribes.
Ellicott calls it a singular collocation, the laity set between priests; Keil places the names in the ordered file of princes.
Henry sees the whole society, not the clergy only, giving thanks.

themes: Judah and Benjamin as men not tribes
the whole nation as one company

schools.summary: Gill fixes the priests' sons with trumpets, the trumpet being the priestly instrument.

Keil traces Zechariah's descent from Asaph, the Davidic instruments (1 Chron. 23:5; 2 Chron. 29:26), and reckons seven trumpeters per company (v.41); Ellicott insists nothing deviated from sacred precedent.

Keil sets the Davidic instruments and the ascent by the stairs of the city of David (Neh. 3:15), owning the topography not quite intelligible; Ellicott gives Ezra the scribe his place before them, greatest in dignity though second in office.
Gill takes 'his brethren' for the brethren of Zechariah, the file of players.
Keil traces the ascent by the stairs of the city of David to the water gate, owning the statements not now quite intelligible; Ellicott marks the shorter eastern route and the fidelity to precedent.
Gill sets the fountain gate south of the dung gate where the procession began.

themes: the route of the first company
the fountain gate and the stairs

schools.summary: Keil traces the second company's route from the tower of the furnaces to the broad wall; Ellicott gives it the longer northern round by the sheep gate to the prison gate (cf. Neh. 3).
Clarke supposes the broad wall a public promenade or a parade for the temple guard.
Gill sets the second company on the northern part of the wall.
Henry marks Nehemiah bringing up the rear as Ezra led the van.
Ellicott notes the gate of Ephraim was not repaired (Neh. 3), having remained comparatively intact with the broad wall; Keil carries the file of gates and towers to the sheep gate.
Gill fixes the gate of Ephraim, so named as leading toward that tribe.
Wesley reads the halt as waiting, that the two companies might enter the house of God together in due order.

themes: the halt at the prison gate

schools.summary: Ellicott reads that they stood first outside and then entered, the main worship being under the open heavens; Keil records the two companies standing in the house of God.
Gill marks the companies meeting in the great court, for no lesser space could hold them.
Henry: both companies met and joined their thanksgivings, Nehemiah with the half of the rulers.

themes: the two companies meet in the temple

schools.summary: Ellicott marks the names as personal, not found in the earlier lists; Keil reckons seven priests here, matching the first company's trumpeters.
Gill notes the priests stood there also, whose names the verse gives.

themes: the symmetry of the two companies

schools.summary: Keil fixes the singers singing loud under Jezrahiah their overseer; Ellicott insists nothing departed from the sacred forms of David.
Gill takes the eight names for priests who blew the trumpets.

Henry paints the loud shouts of the common people heard afar, accepted by a God who overlooks not the zeal of mean people; God himself made them rejoice, and the baffled malice of their enemies added to the joy.
Ellicott marks the verse full of joy, yet the abundant sacrifice coming before the rejoicing.
Gill reads the great sacrifices as many peace offerings on which the people feasted, a festival day.
Wesley notes the wives and children rejoicing, their hosannas recorded to their praise.

themes: the joy of Jerusalem heard afar off
God the author of the joy

schools.summary: Henry reads the appointment as the good fruit of a thanksgiving that leaves ministers and people more careful, some set to gather the dues lest the ministers' portion be lost for want of demanding.
Keil sets the joint work of Nehemiah and Ezra restoring the law's enactments; Ellicott the temple service restored to Davidical completeness, the people providing amply.
Gill notes overseers of the treasuries appointed on the very day of the dedication.
Wesley: the people rejoiced for the ministers' gifts and the provision made, that they might wholly wait upon their office.

themes: ministers who wait on their office

schools.summary: Keil reads the singers and porters keeping their office punctually according to the command of David and Solomon (2 Chron. 8:14); Ellicott glosses 'keep the ward' as observing the regular seasons of sacrifice and thanksgiving.
Gill fixes the singers keeping their courses and the porters guarding the gates against the unclean.
Wesley reads 'the ward' as the charge God prescribed, and chiefly the charge of purification.
Henry finds the joy of the dedication quickening the ministers to diligence in their work.
Gill sets the chief singers of David and Asaph over the rest, with Heman and Jeduthun, to instruct and order the music.
Keil reads the current arrangement as continuing what David and Asaph established of old; Ellicott catches the reverence shown for the old precedents.

Clarke traces the chain from the people through the Levites to the priests, 'sanctifying' meaning dedicating to holy use; Wesley presses the conscience that set apart firstfruits and tithes and would not profane holy things.
Ellicott sets the Levites between people and priests, receiving the tithe and giving the priests their tithe of the tithe (Num. 18:26).
Gill notes the punctual payment of the Levites' dues under Zerubbabel and Nehemiah.
Henry: the holy things, given with an eye to God, are sanctified and bring the blessing to rest on the house (Ezek. 44:30).
